young.html: C. H. Waddington was a British biologist who wondered about one of the most amazing things in nature: how does a single, tiny cell, a fertilized egg, turn into a whole body, with nerves, skin, muscles and blood, all in the right places?

Every cell in your body carries the same set of genes. So why does one cell become a nerve and another a muscle? Waddington drew a famous picture to explain it. Imagine a ball at the top of a hilly landscape, with valleys branching as they go down. The ball is a young cell. As it rolls, it must choose a valley at each fork, and at the bottom each valley ends in a different kind of cell.

young.name: gb-landscape
young.cap: Set the signals and roll a cell down the valleys. Then roll 20 at once. Make the valleys shallow and see how often cells go astray.

young.html: Build a landscape. Crumple a sheet of aluminum foil, then smooth it over a towel so you get hills and grooves. Tilt it a little and roll a marble or a dried pea from the top several times. Does it usually end up in the same groove? Press one groove deeper with your finger and try again. Waddington called deep, reliable grooves canalization.

full.html: Conrad Hal Waddington (1905–1975) studied at Cambridge, first geology and then embryology and genetics, and from 1947 to 1970 was professor of animal genetics at the University of Edinburgh. He was one of the first biologists to try to join genetics, the study of embryos and evolution into a single picture. He also wrote widely on science, art and society.

The Nature of Life (1961) is his short book for general readers. It explains what genes are, how a body develops from an egg, and how evolution works, and argues that the three questions can’t be understood apart.
This book was first published in 1961, so it is still under copyright, and this rung quotes none of it. Everything here is our own summary.

full.text: The question: from genes to a body

full.html: By 1961 DNA had been shown to carry genes (its structure was found in 1953). But genes alone don’t explain a body. Nearly every cell carries the same genes. A liver cell and a nerve cell differ because different genes are switched on in them, and that depends on the cell’s history and surroundings in the embryo. Waddington coined the word epigenetics (1942) for the study of how genes act during development to produce the body’s traits.

His most famous picture is a sloping landscape of branching valleys. A ball rolling down stands for a developing cell. The shape of the hills is set by the action of many genes pulling together, like guy ropes under a tent. At each fork, small signals from neighboring cells tip the ball one way or the other; once in a valley, it is hard to climb out.

full.name: gb-landscape
full.cap: Development as rolling downhill. The depth of the valleys is canalization: deep valleys give the same result despite small upsets.

full.html: Canalization: development is buffered, so that organisms come out much the same despite small differences in their genes or surroundings. The valleys are deep. Only a strong push, or a change in many genes, sends a cell into a different valley.

Waddington tested a bold idea. In the early 1950s he gave fruit-fly pupae a short heat shock. Some grew up with a gap in a small wing vein (a “crossveinless” wing). He bred only from those flies, generation after generation, and shocked each new batch. After a number of generations, some flies showed the trait without any heat shock. Selection had reshaped the landscape, so that a trait first produced by the environment became built in. He called this genetic assimilation. It works through ordinary selection on hidden genetic variation, not through inheritance of acquired traits.

full.title: Cells from one egg
full.q: A fertilized egg divides into 2 cells, then 4, then 8, and so on. If every cell divided each time, how many rounds of division would make about 35 trillion cells, roughly the number in a human body?
full.a: About 45 rounds. Growth is fast; the hard part is making each cell the right kind in the right place.

full.title: How reliable is development?
full.q: Suppose at each of two forks a cell follows its signal with probability 0.95. What is the chance it reaches the intended kind? What if the valleys are shallow, so the chance at each fork is only 0.7?
full.a: Canalization matters: small losses at each fork multiply.

full.html: In the book’s later chapters Waddington argues that evolution is not only genes and selection. The way genes act in development, and the way animals choose and change their surroundings by their behavior, help decide what natural selection can work on. He also discusses what makes something alive and argues that biology needs its own concepts, such as development and organization, alongside those of physics and chemistry.

Confusing Waddington with Lamarck. Waddington did not claim that traits acquired in a lifetime are passed on directly. In genetic assimilation, selection picks out flies whose genes make the trait easier to produce, until some produce it unaided.

For some decades Waddington’s ideas were somewhat at the edge of biology, which was busy with DNA and molecules. They have since come back strongly. Biologists now map the gene networks that make the valleys of his landscape, and stem-cell researchers use his picture to explain how cells can be pushed back uphill (Shinya Yamanaka’s 2006 discovery of how to turn adult cells back into stem cells earned a Nobel Prize in 2012). The word epigenetics has taken on a narrower modern meaning too, for chemical marks on DNA and its packaging that switch genes on and off. Debates continue about how much development and behavior should be added to the standard account of evolution.

items: Aristotle and Harvey, earlier on this ladder, asked whether an embryo is preformed or built step by step (Harvey’s word was epigenesis, the root of Waddington’s “epigenetics”).
Darwin and Dobzhansky explained how populations change; Waddington asks how changed genes become changed bodies.
Schrödinger asked what a gene is; Waddington asks what genes do together.
If every cell has the same genes, what makes them different?
Is a body more like a machine built from a blueprint, or like a river finding its course?
Can a trait be both inherited and shaped by the environment? How?

questions: You started as one cell. What does it feel like to think about that?
Why might it be good for living things to develop the same way even when conditions change a little?
Waddington’s landscape is a picture, not a real place. How can a picture help scientists think?
Identical twins have the same genes. In what ways can they still differ?
Waddington wanted biology, physics and chemistry to work together. What problems need several kinds of experts?
